# Making Modal your own {#sec-customisation}

Customisation is another use of the command language. A setting can be tried
live, then kept as a startup command when it proves useful. The built-in
bindings and themes remain available underneath the personal choices.

There are three homes for information: the song holds musical decisions,
the configuration file holds deliberate application preferences, and the
machine's state files hold things Modal remembers for itself.

## Trying a setting and keeping it

At the `:` prompt, `set NAME=VALUE` changes a setting immediately. A question
mark asks for its current value: `:set fontsize?`. Several settings can appear
on one line, such as `:set fontsize=14 hintdelay=200`.

Boolean settings also have short forms: `:set audition` enables audition,
`:set noaudition` disables it and `:set audition!` toggles it. The `!` here
belongs to the setting word. It is different from the bang after a file
command, such as `:w! FILE`.

The `modalrc` file contains startup commands, one per line. Modal runs its
built-in defaults first, then this file. A few chosen lines are usually
better than copying every default: settings left unspecified continue to
follow future defaults.

```text
" Comments begin with a double quote
set fontsize=14
set hintdelay=200
set theme=light
```

`:write-config` opens a save dialogue in the configuration directory. With
a filename, `:write-config modalrc` writes there directly, refusing an
existing file unless `:write-config! modalrc` is used. The generated file
writes changed choices as commands and leaves unchanged defaults commented,
with descriptions. It is a useful starting point rather than a file that
must be maintained in full.

`:source` with no filename runs `modalrc` again. It applies those commands
over the current state; deleting a line from the file does not reverse a
change already made in the running application. Restarting begins again
from the defaults before applying the remaining lines.

## File locations

| Kind | Linux | Windows |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Configuration | `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/modal`, normally `~/.config/modal` | `%APPDATA%\Modal` |
| State | `$XDG_STATE_HOME/modal`, normally `~/.local/state/modal` | `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Modal` |

Personal themes live in `themes/` inside the configuration directory.
The state directory's `ports` file remembers this machine's enabled ports,
aliases and defaults. Those choices belong to the Ports view, not to `modalrc`.
Its `remembered` file retains palette ranking, macros and other remembered
choices. It is not the song file.

A startup-command error names its file and line on the message row. Later
lines still run, so one spelling mistake does not suppress the whole
configuration. On Linux, errors also appear on standard error.

Application preferences and the machine's port choices are separate from
song edits: `u` is not a general undo for every configuration change. Ports
are remembered as they are changed in the Ports view. `:palette-forget`
clears the palette's learned ranking without changing the song.

## Naming a custom scale

Key-aware transforms can use a scale defined in the configuration. The
`scale` command gives it a name and ascending degrees, for example:

```text
scale Hijaz 1 b2 3 4 5 b6 b7
```

The degrees describe a scale relative to its tonic, so the same definition
can be used in different keys. This extends the available musical vocabulary
without changing the semitone movement keys or creating a global scale lock.
The definition belongs in `modalrc` when it should be available at startup.

## Choosing a readable view

Ctrl-plus and Ctrl-minus change text size, and Ctrl-0 returns to the configured
size. The window keeps its pixel size, showing more or fewer character cells.
A larger font therefore trades the amount visible for easier reading.

`font` chooses a local TrueType or OpenType file; an empty value uses the
built-in JetBrains Mono. The window's character grid remains fixed-width
in its layout. `minsize` sets the smallest permitted size in cells, rather
than prescribing one physical display size.

Settings that influence feedback include `hints`, `hintdelay`, `timeoutlen`
and `palettelines`. Hint delay controls when a menu appears. Timeout length
is a different matter: when one bound sequence is also the start of a longer
one, it limits how long Modal waits before running the shorter. Making hints
quicker need not make the keyboard timeout shorter.

The complete settings table, with actual defaults, is in
@sec-settings-reference. Musical properties such as the track's grid or
recording lead-in have their own fields or commands and are not all `set`
variables.

## Themes describe roles

A theme assigns colours to **roles**, such as note, cursor, selection and
warning. It does not paint individual notes by arbitrary colour commands.
This keeps the same meaning recognisable across views.

`:set theme=dark` and `:set theme=light` choose the built-in themes. A personal
theme is a command file in `themes/NAME`, containing only the roles it changes.
It starts from the dark theme before applying its overrides. For example:

```text
highlight cursor #e0af68
highlight note #9ece6a
highlight selection #2e3c64
```

`highlight` commands after `set theme` override that theme in turn. `:write-config`
lists the colours of all the roles in the chosen theme, providing names and
values to start from. Keep enough contrast to distinguish the cursor,
selected material, search matches and playback; their different purposes
are more useful than a colour scheme that makes them look alike.

## Key bindings attach names to actions

A key binding names a command. `nmap` binds Normal-mode keys; an optional
hint supplies the label shown in the key menus. `nunmap` removes a binding.

```text
nmap <F6> view-piano-roll "Piano roll"
```

This binds another route to the existing view command; it does not create a
new kind of piano roll. The named command can also be found in the palette.
A command's context still applies: binding a note operation to another key
does not make it meaningful in the Ports view.

A personal binding is also useful when a command has no default arrow-key
alternative. For example, these add Alt-arrow section reordering on the
section strip, alongside its default `Alt-h` and `Alt-l` bindings:

```text
nmap <A-Left> section-move-earlier "Move a section earlier"
nmap <A-Right> section-move-later "Move a section later"
```

The commands apply only on the strip, so the existing Alt-arrow note movements
in the piano roll retain their own context.

Keys in configuration use angle-bracket notation for named or modified
keys: `<Esc>`, `<Tab>`, `<CR>` for Enter, `<Space>`, `<C-p>` for Ctrl-P and
`<A-Left>` for Alt-Left (`<A-h>` for the letter alternative). Ordinary sequences
run together: `gg`, or `<C-w>` followed by Down (or `j`).
A literal less-than sign is `<lt>`. `<leader>` means the current leader,
so bindings written with it follow a change to the `leader` setting.

For example, `set leader=<Space>` moves the leader groups to Space. That
choice changes a prominent existing binding, so it is worth considering
how playback will then be reached. The live key list shows what the resolved
bindings actually do in the current context.

Bindings may share a key when their commands apply in different places,
as `J` already does for octave movement and section joining. A later
applicable binding overrides an earlier one. `ngroup` gives a prefix a hint
menu title; `keysection` groups subsequent bindings in the list of keys.
Advanced map forms exist for other modes, but not every proposed editing
mode is implemented; the current grammar remains the guide to actual use.

Arguments with spaces are quoted. Within a command file, `\"` represents a
quote and `\\` a backslash. This is command-file quoting, distinct from the
rules of a terminal such as PowerShell. Using the file chooser or completion
avoids manually escaping many file paths.

Customisation works best when it supports already-understood operations.
The standard bindings in this book remain a common vocabulary; the live
menus and palette provide the corresponding vocabulary for a customised setup.
